options: Sole over pressure points (heel, metatarsal heads)
Inner lower leg above the ankle (gaiter area)

history.ask: Pain in the ulcer and the limb
options: Painless ulcer — patient walked on it unaware
Pain at rest, worse elevating the leg, relieved hanging it down
Aching worse standing, relieved by elevation
Pain after a fixed short distance, relieved by rest

history.ask: Numbness, burning, or tingling in the feet
options: Yes — glove-and-stocking numbness or burning at night

history.ask: A red hot swollen foot without a wound
options: Yes — swollen warm foot, little pain
Edge became raised, heaped, or bleeds easily after years

red_flags: Spreading sepsis with crepitus, blistering, or wet gangrene — limb- and life-threatening; urgent surgical referral
Rest pain with a cold, pulseless, pale foot — critical limb ischemia; urgent surgical referral
Systemic toxicity (fever, rigors, confusion) from a foot ulcer
Probe reaching bone in an ulcer with fever — deep sepsis with likely bone involvement
A red, hot, swollen, minimally painful foot in a neuropathic patient without a wound — acute Charcot foot, easily mislabeled as cellulitis
exam: Describe the ulcer precisely: site, size, depth, edge (punched-out, sloping, raised/everted), base, and discharge
Probe the ulcer gently with a sterile probe — reaching bone strongly supports osteomyelitis
Palpate dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial, popliteal, and femoral pulses on both sides
Compare foot temperature and capillary refill between sides
Test protective sensation with a 10 g monofilament at standard plantar points, plus vibration sense
Inspect for deformity — claw toes, prominent metatarsal heads, rocker-bottom collapse of the arch
Look between the toes and under callus for hidden breakdown; inspect the footwear the patient came in
Feel for crepitus, fluctuance, and tracking pus around the ulcer
Look for venous skin change — varicosities, hemosiderin staining, lipodermatosclerosis around a gaiter-area ulcer
Record temperature and vitals when infection is suspected
Measure ankle-brachial pressure with a hand Doppler if available — interpret cautiously, calcified diabetic vessels read falsely high

investigations.why: Confirms and grades the diabetes driving neuropathic ulceration and poor healing; may diagnose diabetes for the first time in an 'unknown' ulcer
Leukocytosis supports spreading infection or deep sepsis over an uninfected neuropathic or venous ulcer
A persistently high ESR under an ulcer supports osteomyelitis; CRP tracks acute soft-tissue infection
Diabetic nephropathy travels with the foot disease and must be known before any contrast imaging
Identifies the organisms in an infected ulcer — deep tissue, not a surface swab, reflects the true flora
First-line for bone: destruction supports osteomyelitis, gas in soft tissue supports necrotizing infection, and joint fragmentation supports Charcot foot

investigations.test: Arterial Doppler / duplex of the limb
investigations.why: Separates the ischemic ulcer (needing vascular referral) from the purely neuropathic one — the single most management-defining split in this pathway

investigations.test: Edge biopsy of a chronic non-healing ulcer
investigations.why: Rules in Marjolin's (squamous cell) transformation when the edge has become raised or friable after years
Second-line — if X-ray is normal but osteomyelitis or deep abscess is still suspected: shows the earliest bone marrow change and maps deep collections
